title: AustralianSuper backs performance test rethink for VC
full_text:
AustralianSuper has backed further work on a performance test benchmark for emerging assets, arguing the framework should reflect venture capital’s (VC) longer investment lifecycle.
The Treasury’s May 2026 consultation considered possible changes to the superannuation performance test for emerging and alternative assets while maintaining its focus on protecting member outcomes.
AustralianSuper head of private equity, APAC, Lilian Fang said the fund supported further consideration of a benchmark suited to investments whose returns may initially be low before increasing later in their lifecycle.
“We’re supportive of further work on a well-designed benchmark for emerging assets, provided it reflects how these investments develop over time and doesn’t create an expectation that funds allocate members’ savings to particular asset classes.
“The performance test is one of many factors in our investment decisions, but not a material constraint on our VC portfolio. Our focus remains on the quality of the opportunities available, disciplined portfolio construction and delivering strong long-term outcomes for members.”
AustralianSuper has committed more than $1.5 billion to Australian VC, up from about $600 million five years ago. Through its investment managers, the fund has gained exposure to more than 250 Australian start-ups since 2016 and seven of the nine local unicorns currently valued at US$1 billion or more.
The VC holdings account for less than 0.5 per cent of AustralianSuper’s portfolio, which manages more than $430 billion for 3.6 million members.
Fang said the portfolio remained relatively young and its performance needed to be assessed over longer periods rather than individual quarters or years.
“Over the long term, though, it has outperformed the S&P/ASX 300 Accumulation Index by a comfortable margin.
“That’s an encouraging result. Of course, it needs to be considered in the context of the portfolio’s maturity and the nature of the asset class. VC valuations and returns can move significantly as market conditions change, and a large part of the value in younger funds may remain unrealised for some time.”
AustralianSuper has built its exposure through managers including Blackbird, Square Peg and AirTree Ventures, with diversification spanning companies, sectors, development stages and investment periods.
Higher interest rates have increased pressure on valuations and placed greater emphasis on revenue quality and the path to profitability, but Fang said the fund did not automatically reduce its VC exposure when conditions tightened.
“Our approach is to make commitments over different periods rather than attempting to predict the top or bottom of the cycle. This provides exposure to different investment vintages, while our pace of investment and selection process remain responsive to valuations, financing conditions and the quality of opportunities available.”
AI has also reshaped the opportunity set, with its share of Australian VC investment rising from 7 per cent during the 2020–22 investment boom to 23 per cent. Australia had more than 470 venture capital-backed AI start-ups valued collectively at US$34.9 billion as at May 2026.
Despite the potential exposure to emerging technologies, Fang said prospective returns still needed to compensate members for the risks, costs, illiquidity and time involved.
“For us, the question is not whether every company in our VC portfolio succeeds, but whether the portfolio as a whole is delivering an appropriate long-term outcome for members after accounting for risk and costs. To date, the answer to that question is an unequivocal yes.”
author: Adrian Suljanovic
